overview:
In Jain philosophical vocabulary, “disliking” can be examined through several related concepts: *dveṣa* (aversion), *pratigha* (anger‑based repulsion), and the broader triad of *kaṣāyas* (passions) that shape mental states. Jainism does not treat disliking as a moral fault in itself; rather, it distinguishes between ordinary evaluative preference—an everyday cognitive response—and ethically charged aversion that binds karma. The tradition emphasizes that disliking becomes spiritually consequential when it escalates into reactive hostility, attachment to one’s own preferences, or actions that harm oneself or others.

Within the Jain analysis of mind, disliking is understood as a conditioned response arising from past karmic impressions (*saṃskāras*) and present cognitive habits. It is not inherently sinful, but it can become a doorway to *dveṣa*, one of the principal causes of karmic influx (*āsrava*). The Tattvārtha Sūtra and canonical Āgamas describe how aversion arises when the mind reacts to perceived unpleasantness, leading to agitation, verbal harshness, or physical harm. The ethical project of Jainism is not to suppress all forms of preference but to cultivate awareness, equanimity (*samatā*), and non‑reactivity so that disliking does not mature into harmful passion.

Different Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—agree on the basic structure of aversion as a karmically binding passion but offer distinct pedagogical emphases. Digambara commentaries often highlight the subtlety of *dveṣa* as a mental vibration that disturbs the soul’s natural purity. Śvetāmbara sources frequently frame disliking within the broader discipline of *ahiṃsā*, noting that aversion can lead to micro‑violence in speech and thought. Modern Jain ethics interprets disliking through psychological lenses, encouraging laypeople to recognize emotional triggers, practice mindful restraint, and cultivate compassion even toward disliked persons or situations.

In everyday life, disliking is treated as a natural human experience. Jain lay practice guides do not demand the elimination of all negative feelings but encourage reflective awareness: noticing the feeling, understanding its causes, and preventing it from escalating into harmful action. This approach aligns with the broader Jain commitment to non‑violence, self‑knowledge, and gradual reduction of passions across the *guṇasthānas* (spiritual stages).

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.3 identifies *dveṣa* as one of the four primary passions (*kaṣāyas*). Commentaries (Digambara and Śvetāmbara) explain that disliking becomes karmically significant when it develops into reactive hostility.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.original_text: जहा दुहं तहा दव्वं, जहा दव्वं तहा दुहं
primary_sources.transliteration: jahā duhaṃ tahā davvaṃ, jahā davvaṃ tahā duhaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Where there is suffering, there is hostility; where there is hostility, there is suffering.
primary_sources.notes: This passage (Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2) links aversion and hostility to the cycle of suffering. It does not condemn ordinary disliking but warns against the escalation into harmful mental states.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: Faults arise from anger and aversion.
primary_sources.notes: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11 discusses how aversion (*dveṣa*) contributes to mental disturbances and unethical behavior. The text emphasizes awareness and restraint.

misconceptions.myth: Jainism teaches that all forms of disliking are spiritually harmful.
misconceptions.reality: Primary texts distinguish between ordinary preference and karmically binding aversion. Only when disliking escalates into reactive hostility or harmful passion does it generate negative karma.

misconceptions.myth: A Jain practitioner must suppress all negative emotions, including disliking.
misconceptions.reality: Jain ethics encourages mindful awareness, not suppression. The goal is to prevent disliking from maturing into anger, cruelty, or violence.
Ahiṃsā concerns harm in thought, speech, and action. Disliking becomes relevant to ahiṃsā only when it leads to harmful intentions or behaviors.
